newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran president candidates want U.S. out of Gulf.
newsitem.headline: Iran president candidates want U.S. out of Gulf.

text.p: The two leading candidates in Iran's presidential election have said they would aim to bring about the departure of U.S. military forces from the oil-rich Gulf region.

Parliamentary Speaker Ali Nateq-Nouri and former culture minister Mohammad Khatami said that Tehran would try to convince its Gulf Arab neighbours that Iran did not pose a threat to them, removing the need for the U.S. presence.

"The first thing is to develop relations with Persian Gulf countries...By convincing them that the Islamic republic is not a threat to them we could push away the enemy," Nateq-Nouri said in a televised presidential debate late on Tuesday.
"The security of this (Gulf) family should be provided by its members, not America," said Nateq-Nouri, the candidate most tipped to win Friday's election.
There are some 20,000 U.S. troops deployed in and around the Gulf which is the base for the Fifth Fleet. Part of the forces are used to enforce United Nations sanctions against Iraq.
The United States has vowed to protect its Gulf Arab allies from any potential Iranian security threat.

Washington has accused the Tehran government of sponsoring international terrorism. Iran has repeatedly denied the charges and has accused the United States of stoking regional tensions to sell its allies billions of dollars in high-tech arms.

Mohammad Khatami, who according to one opinion poll published on Thursday is leading the race, said that the removal of U.S. forces would guarantee stability in the region and ensure Iran's independence.

"Pushing away the enemy and its fleet from the region would guarantee our independence...All our efforts should be concentrated on convincing everybody and using all international and national levers so that the enemy would leave," Khatami said in the televised debate.

U.S. forces tracked Iranian naval and military exercises this month and officials have previously warned its Gulf allies that Iran has built up a capacity to threaten the strategic Strait of Hormuz which carries 20 percent of the world's oil.

Iran's conservative Sunni Gulf neighbours such as oil-giants Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates have eyed radical Shi'ite Iran with suspicion, with relations marred by accusations of internal meddling and territorial disputes.

But relations between the Gulf Cooperation Council -- a six member political and economic grouping of Gulf states -- and non-Arab Iran have improved this year, resulting in the GCC welcoming Iranian steps to improve relations.
Iran says that the presence of U.S. forces in the Gulf is the biggest threat to regional security.

"America is selling arms and taking money away from these countries by demonising Iran and pretending to guard their security while it is the very cause of insecurity in the region," Nateq-Nouri said.
Iranian President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani is standing down as president after serving the two four-year terms permitted under the Iranian constitution.
